the complexin proteins are significantly decreased in Alzheimer's disease and that the APOE 4 allele may exacerbate the synaptic loss in Alzheimer's disease.

the presynaptic proteins are not reduced in AD and the presynaptic and postsynaptic proteins are reduced in APOE epsilon4 carriers, and that the presynaptically localized complexins are reduced in AD.
the relative loss of presynaptic terminal protein in AD is not a general phenomenon but is specific to inhibitory synapse, and that the relative loss is greater in APOE epsilon4 carriers.

synaptic proteins that have been implicated in the pathogenesis of AD.
the role of the presynaptic proteins complexin I, complexin II, and synaptophysin in Alzheimer's disease.
the role of synaptic proteins in the pathophysiology of AD and in the APOE 4 risk for AD.

synaptic dysfunction is a pathological feature of AD, but the loss of synaptophysin and complexins is not a general feature of AD.
the loss of synaptic proteins is a characteristic feature of AD, and is more severe in cases carrying APOE epsilon4.
synaptic proteins are lost in the hippocampus, inferior temporal cortex, and occipital cortex of AD patients.

the presynaptic proteins are lost selectively and that there is an increased loss with APOE epsilon4.

The main takeaway from our work is that

the loss of synaptic proteins, particularly the inhibitory synapse protein complexin I, is a pathological feature of Alzheimer’s disease (AD), and the loss is greater in AD cases carrying the APOE 4 allele.
there is a relative loss of presynaptic and postsynaptic proteins in Alzheimer's brain, which may be a feature of the disease.
the presynaptic proteins are not affected by AD, but the postsynaptic proteins are affected.
